claim: Neural activity in auditory cortex tracks the amplitude-onset envelope of continuous speech.
source: Neural activity in auditory cortex tracks the amplitude-onset envelope of continuous speech, but recent work counterintuitively suggests that neural tracking increases when speech is masked by background noise, despite reduced speech intelligibility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural tracking increases when speech is masked by background noise, despite reduced speech intelligibility.
source: Neural activity in auditory cortex tracks the amplitude-onset envelope of continuous speech, but recent work counterintuitively suggests that neural tracking increases when speech is masked by background noise, despite reduced speech intelligibility.
evidence: Referenced as recent work and demonstrated in the current experiments.

claim: Neural speech tracking is enhanced for speech masked by background noise at very high signal-to-noise ratios (~30 dB SNR) where speech is highly intelligible.
source: Results show that (1) neural speech tracking is enhanced for speech masked by background noise at very high signal-to-noise ratios (~30 dB SNR) where speech is highly intelligible
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental data in Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The neural tracking enhancement due to background noise is independent of attention.
source: (2) this enhancement is independent of attention
evidence: Demonstrated in Experiment 2 where participants performed a visual task while ignoring speech.

claim: The neural tracking enhancement generalizes across different stationary background maskers, but is strongest for 12-talker babble.
source: (3) it generalizes across different stationary background maskers, but is strongest for 12-talker babble
evidence: Demonstrated through comparisons across masker types in Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: The neural tracking enhancement is present for headphone and free-field listening.
source: (4) it is present for headphone and free-field listening, suggesting that the neural-tracking enhancement generalizes to real-life listening.
evidence: Demonstrated in Experiment 5 comparing headphone and loudspeaker presentation.

claim: Minimal background noise enhances the neural representation of the speech onset-envelope.
source: The work paints a clear picture that minimal background noise enhances the neural representation of the speech onset-envelope, suggesting that stochastic resonance contributes to neural speech tracking.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the pattern of results across all five experiments.

claim: Stochastic resonance contributes to neural speech tracking.
source: The work paints a clear picture that minimal background noise enhances the neural representation of the speech onset-envelope, suggesting that stochastic resonance contributes to neural speech tracking.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of results showing noise-related enhancement independent of attention.

claim: Background noise induces non-linearities in neural tracking that make its use as a biological marker for speech processing challenging.
source: The work further highlights non-linearities of neural tracking induced by background noise that make its use as a biological marker for speech processing challenging.
evidence: Inferred from the complex relationship between SNR and neural tracking observed across experiments.

claim: Speech comprehension challenges are a serious barrier to social participation.
source: Speech comprehension challenges are a serious barrier to social participation (Nachtegaal et al., 2009; Heffernan et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Speech comprehension challenges can have long-term negative health consequences, such as cognitive decline.
source: Speech comprehension challenges are a serious barrier to social participation (Nachtegaal et al., 2009; Heffernan et al., 2016) and can have long-term negative health consequences, such as cognitive decline (Lin and Albert, 2014; Panza et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Greater speech tracking has been associated with higher speech intelligibility.
source: Greater speech tracking has been associated with higher speech intelligibility (Ding et al., 2014; Vanthornhout et al., 2018; Lesenfants et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Speech tracking could be a useful clinical biomarker, for example, in individuals with hearing loss.
source: Greater speech tracking has been associated with higher speech intelligibility (Ding et al., 2014; Vanthornhout et al., 2018; Lesenfants et al., 2019), leading to the suggestion that speech tracking could be a useful clinical biomarker, for example, in individuals with hearing loss (Gillis et al., 2022; Palana et al., 2022; Schmitt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a suggestion from previous literature, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Neural speech tracking increases in the presence of background masking sound even at masking levels for which speech intelligibility is decreased.
source: Counterintuitively, however, neural speech tracking has been shown to increase in the presence of background masking sound even at masking levels for which speech intelligibility is decreased (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) between speech and background noise, neural speech tracking decreases relative to high SNRs.
source: For low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) between speech and background noise, neural speech tracking decreases relative to high SNRs (Ding and Simon, 2013; Vanthornhout et al., 2018; Zou et al., 2019; Yasmin et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: For speech in moderate background noise, when a listener can understand most words, neural speech tracking can be increased relative to clear speech.
source: In contrast, for speech in moderate background noise, when a listener can understand most words, neural speech tracking can be increased relative to clear speech (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: The neural-tracking increase for speech in moderate background noise has been interpreted to reflect the increased attention required to understand speech.
source: This has been interpreted to reflect the increased attention required to understand speech (Hauswald et al., 2022; Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an interpretation from previous literature, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Stochastic resonance is a phenomenon where background noise amplifies the response of a system to an input.
source: However, the low-to-moderate SNRs (e.g., <10 dB) typically used to study neural speech tracking require listeners to invest cognitively and thus do not allow distinguishing a cognitive mechanism from the possibility that the noise per se leads to an increase in neural tracking, for example, through stochastic resonance, where background noise amplifies the response of a system to an input (Kitajo et al., 2007; McDonnell and Ward, 2011; Krauss et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The neural-tracking increase has been observed for speech masked by multi-talker background babble.
source: For example, the neural-tracking increase has been observed for speech masked by multi-talker background babble (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: The neural-tracking increase appears to be less present for noise that spectrally matches the speech signal.
source: but appears to be less present for noise that spectrally matches the speech signal (Ding and Simon, 2013; Synigal et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: Neural responses to tone bursts can increase in the presence of minimal noise (i.e., high SNRs) relative to clear conditions.
source: Other research indicates that neural responses to tone bursts can increase in the presence of minimal noise (i.e., high SNRs) relative to clear conditions (Alain et al., 2009; Alain et al., 2012; Alain et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Older adults often exhibit enhanced neural speech tracking.
source: Moreover, older adults often exhibit enhanced neural speech tracking (Presacco et al., 2016; Brodbeck et al., 2018b; Broderick et al., 2021; Panela et al., 2024)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The age-related neural-tracking enhancement is thought to be due to a loss of inhibition and increased internal noise.
source: Moreover, older adults often exhibit enhanced neural speech tracking (Presacco et al., 2016; Brodbeck et al., 2018b; Broderick et al., 2021; Panela et al., 2024) which is thought to be due to a loss of inhibition and increased internal noise (Zeng, 2013; Auerbach et al., 2014; Krauss et al., 2016; Zeng, 2020; Herrmann and Butler, 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation from previous literature, cited in the manuscript.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants listened to ~2 min stories either in quiet (clear) or in the presence of 12-talker background babble at SNRs ranging from highly intelligible (+30 dB SNR) to moderately difficult intelligibility (−2 dB SNR).
source: Participants (N = 22, median age: 23.5 years) listened to ~2 min stories either in quiet (clear) or in the presence of 12-talker background babble at SNRs ranging from highly intelligible (+30 dB SNR) to moderately difficult intelligibility (−2 dB SNR) while EEG was recorded.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: Speech at SNRs above ~12 dB is as intelligible as clear speech.
source: Previous work demonstrated that speech at SNRs above ~12 dB is as intelligibility as clear speech (Holder et al., 2018; Rowland et al., 2018; Spyridakou et al., 2020; Irsik et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gist ratings for sentences have been shown to correlate highly with intelligibility (word report).
source: Gist ratings for sentences have been shown to correlate highly with intelligibility (word report; Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Ritz et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Experiment 1, comprehension accuracy and gist ratings did not differ between clear speech and any of the SNR levels.
source: Comprehension accuracy and gist ratings did not differ between clear speech and any of the SNR levels (pFDR > 0.05; thresholded using false discover rate [FDR]; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Genovese et al., 2002; Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +15.6 dB SNR, such that gist ratings decreased for +15.6 dB SNR and lower.
source: The piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +15.6 dB SNR, such that gist ratings decreased for +15.6 dB SNR and lower (t21 = 3.008, p = 0.007, d = 0.641; right to left in Figure 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, gist ratings did not change for +15.6 dB SNR and above.
source: whereas gist ratings did not change for +15.6 dB SNR and above (t21 = 0.214, p = 0.832, d = 0.046).
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, EEG prediction accuracy did not differ between clear speech and any SNR level.
source: EEG prediction accuracy did not differ between clear speech and any SNR level (pFDR > 0.05; Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of EEG data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, the P1-N1 amplitude of the TRF was significantly greater for all SNRs relative to clear speech.
source: In contrast, the P1-N1 amplitude of the TRF was significantly greater for all SNRs relative to clear speech (pFDR ≤ 0.05; Figure 1C, D; results were comparable when using the amplitude envelope instead of the amplitude-onset envelope, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, explorative piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +9.2 dB SNR, showing a significant linear increase in P1-N1 amplitude from +28.4 to +9.2 dB SNR.
source: Explorative piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +9.2 dB SNR, showing a significant linear increase in P1-N1 amplitude from +28.4 to +9.2 dB SNR (right to left in Figure 1D; t21 = –5.131, p = 4.4 ∙ 10–5, d = 1.094)
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of TRF data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, no significant trend was observed for SNRs from about +9.2 to −0.4 dB SNR.
source: whereas no significant trend was observed for SNRs from about +9.2 to −0.4 dB SNR (t21 = 1.001, p = 0.328, d = 0.214).
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of TRF data in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, no differences were found for the P2-N1 amplitude.
source: No differences were found for the P2-N1 amplitude (pFDR > 0.05; Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 1.

claim: Experiment 1 replicates the previously observed enhancement in the neural tracking of the speech onset-envelope for speech presented in moderate background babble.
source: Experiment 1 replicates the previously observed enhancement in the neural tracking of the speech onset-envelope for speech presented in moderate background babble (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in relation to previous literature.

claim: Experiment 1 expands previous work by showing that background babble also leads to enhanced neural speech tracking for very minimal background masking levels (~30 dB SNR).
source: Critically, Experiment 1 expands the previous work by showing that background babble also leads to enhanced neural speech tracking for very minimal background masking levels (~30 dB SNR).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in relation to previous literature.

claim: Speech for very high SNRs (>15 dB) used in Experiment 1 is highly intelligible and thus should require little or no effort to understand.
source: However, speech for very high SNRs (>15 dB) used in Experiment 1 is highly intelligible and thus should require little or no effort to understand.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data and previous literature on speech intelligibility.

claim: It is unlikely that increased attention or effort drive the increase in neural speech tracking in background babble at very high SNRs.
source: It is therefore unlikely that increased attention or effort drive the increase in neural speech tracking in background babble.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing high intelligibility at high SNRs.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants were presented with stories under the same speech-clarity conditions as for Experiment 1 while performing a visual 1-back digit memory task and ignoring the stories.
source: To investigate the role of attention in the noise-related enhancement of neural speech tracking, participants in Experiment 2 (N = 22; median age: 23 years) were presented with stories under the same speech-clarity conditions as for Experiment 1 while performing a visual 1-back digit memory task and ignoring the stories.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, there were no significant differences for hit rate or response time in the visual 1-back task between the clear condition and any of the SNRs.
source: The behavioral results showed no significant differences for hit rate or response time in the visual 1-back task between the clear condition and any of the SNRs (pFDR > 0.05; Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, EEG prediction accuracy did not differ between clear speech and any SNR level.
source: EEG prediction accuracy did not differ between clear speech and any SNR level (pFDR > 0.05; Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of EEG data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the P1-N1 amplitude of the TRF was significantly greater for all SNR levels relative to clear speech.
source: In contrast, and similar to Experiment 1, the P1-N1 amplitude of the TRF was significantly greater for all SNR levels relative to clear speech (pFDR ≤ 0.05; Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, explorative piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +4.4 dB SNR, showing a significant linear increase in P1-N1 amplitude from +28.4 to +4.4 dB SNR.
source: An explorative piece-wise regression revealed a breaking point at +4.4 dB SNR, showing a significant linear increase in P1-N1 amplitude from +28.4 to +4.4 dB SNR (t21 = –3.506, p = 0.002, d = 0.747; right to left in Figure 3D)
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of TRF data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the P1-N1 amplitude decreased from +4.4 to −0.4 dB SNR.
source: whereas the P1-N1 amplitude decreased from +4.4 to −0.4 dB SNR (t21 = 2.416, p = 0.025, d = 0.515).
evidence: Demonstrated through piece-wise regression analysis of TRF data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, no differences were found for the P2-N1 amplitude.
source: No differences were found for the P2-N1 amplitude (pFDR > 0.05; Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no correlation between visual task performance and the noise-related enhancement in P1-N1 amplitude.
source: There was no correlation between visual task performance and the noise-related enhancement in P1-N1 amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), speaking against the possibility that high performers in the visual task expanded effort/attention to speech.
evidence: Demonstrated through correlation analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: The results of Experiment 2 show that, under diverted attention, neural speech tracking is enhanced for speech presented in background babble at very high SNRs (~30 dB SNR) relative to clear speech.
source: The results of Experiment 2 show that, under diverted attention, neural speech tracking is enhanced for speech presented in background babble at very high SNRs (~30 dB SNR) relative to clear speech.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Because participants did not pay attention to the speech in Experiment 2, the results indicate that attention is unlikely to drive the masker-related enhancement in neural tracking.
source: Because participants did not pay attention to the speech in Experiment 2, the results indicate that attention is unlikely to drive the masker-related enhancement in neural tracking observed here and previously (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results of Experiment 2.

claim: The enhancement may be exogenously rather than endogenously driven.
source: The enhancement may thus be exogenously rather than endogenously driven.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of Experiment 2.

claim: A masker-related enhancement was reported for a 12-talker babble masker.
source: A masker-related enhancement was reported for a 12-talker babble masker (Yasmin et al., 2023; Panela et al., 2024)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The masker-related enhancement appears to be absent, or relatively small, for a stationary noise that spectrally matched the speech signal.
source: whereas the effect was absent, or relatively small, for a stationary noise that spectrally matched the speech signal (Ding and Simon, 2013; Zou et al., 2019; Synigal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants listened to stories in quiet (clear), in background babble, and in noise that spectrally matched the speech signal, both at 10, 15, and 20 dB SNR.
source: In Experiment 3, participants listened to stories in quiet (clear), in background babble, and in noise that spectrally matched the speech signal, both at 10, 15, and 20 dB SNR.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, auditory materials were either normalized to the same root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude or the speech signal was kept at the same level across stories and the background sound was added to it at different SNRs.
source: Auditory materials were either normalized to the same root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude (i.e., the intensity of the speech signal decreased with increasing SNR; referred to as 'lower intensity' of speech) or the speech signal was kept at the same level across stories and the background sound was added to it at different SNRs (referred to as 'higher intensity' of the speech).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, comprehension performance and gist ratings were significantly lower, compared to clear speech, for babble-masked speech that was normalized such that the speech level was slightly lower than for clear speech.
source: The analysis of behavioral performance revealed significantly lower comprehension performance and gist ratings, compared to clear speech, for babble-masked speech that was normalized such that the speech level was slightly lower than for clear speech (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for the proportion of correctly answered comprehension questions did not reveal any effects or interactions.
source: The repeated measures analysis of variance (rmANOVA; Masker Type, Normalization Type; excluding clear speech) for the proportion of correctly answered comprehension questions did not reveal any effects or interactions (for all p > 0.1).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for gist ratings revealed an effect of Normalization Type, showing higher gist ratings when the speech signal had a 'higher' compared to a 'lower' intensity.
source: The rmANOVA for gist ratings revealed an effect of Normalization Type (F1,22 = 4.300, p = 0.05, ω2 = 0.008), showing higher gist ratings when the speech signal had a 'higher' compared to a 'lower' intensity, whereas the other effects and interactions were not significant (for all p > 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, EEG prediction accuracy was lower for 15 and 20 dB SNR for the normalization resulting in lower speech intensity relative to clear speech, but otherwise no differences between clear speech and the masked speech.
source: The analysis of EEG prediction accuracy revealed lower accuracies for 15 and 20 dB SNR for the normalization resulting in lower speech intensity relative to clear speech, but otherwise no differences between clear speech and the masked speech (for all pFDR > 0.05; Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of EEG data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for EEG prediction accuracy did not reveal any significant effects nor interactions.
source: The rmANOVA, focusing on the two factors (Normalization Type, Masker Type), did not reveal any significant effects nor interactions (for all p > 0.25).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of EEG data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, for the babble masker, the P1-N1 amplitudes were larger for all SNRs compared to clear speech, for both sound-level normalization types.
source: For the babble masker, the P1-N1 amplitudes were larger for all SNRs compared to clear speech, for both sound-level normalization types (for all pFDR ≤ 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, for the speech-matched noise, P1-N1 amplitudes were larger for all SNRs compared to clear speech for the normalization resulting in lower speech intensity.
source: For the speech-matched noise, P1-N1 amplitudes were larger for all SNRs compared to clear speech for the normalization resulting in lower speech intensity (for all pFDR ≤ 0.05)
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, for the speech-matched noise, P1-N1 amplitudes were larger only for 10 dB SNR for the normalization resulting in higher speech intensity.
source: but only for 10 dB SNR for the normalization resulting in higher speech intensity (15 dB SNR was significant for an uncorrected t-tests).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for P1-N1 amplitude revealed larger P1-N1 amplitudes for the 12-talker babble compared to the speech-matched noise masker.
source: The rmANOVA revealed larger P1-N1 amplitudes for the 12-talker babble compared to the speech-matched noise masker (effect of Masker Type: F1,22 = 32.849, p = 9.1 ∙ 10–6, ω2 = 0.162)
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for P1-N1 amplitude revealed larger amplitudes for lower SNRs.
source: and larger amplitudes for lower SNRs (effect of SNR: F2,44 = 22.608, p = 1.8 ∙ 10–7, ω2 = 0.049).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, none of the interactions nor the effect of Normalization Type were significant for P1-N1 amplitude.
source: None of the interactions nor the effect of Normalization Type were significant (for all p > 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, analysis of the P2-N1 revealed larger amplitudes for speech masked by speech-matched noise at 10 and 15 dB SNR, for both normalization types.
source: Analysis of the P2-N1 revealed larger amplitudes for speech masked by speech-matched noise at 10 and 15 dB SNR, for both normalization types (for all pFDR ≤ 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, none of the other masked speech conditions differed from clear speech for P2-N1 amplitude.
source: None of the other masked speech conditions differed from clear speech.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for P2-N1 amplitude revealed an effect of SNR.
source: The rmANOVA revealed an effect of SNR (F2,44 = 26.851, p = 2.7 ∙ 10–8, ω2 = 0.024)
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for P2-N1 amplitude revealed an effect of Masker Type.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the rmANOVA for P2-N1 amplitude revealed an SNR × Masker Type interaction.
source: and an SNR × Masker Type interaction (F2,44 = 7.684, p = 0.001, ω2 = 0.007).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the SNR × Masker Type interaction for P2-N1 amplitude was due to an increase in P2-N1 amplitude with decreasing SNR for the speech-matched noise.
source: The interaction was due to an increase in P2-N1 amplitude with decreasing SNR for the speech-matched noise (all pHolm ≤ 0.05)
evidence: Demonstrated through post-hoc analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, P2-N1 amplitudes for babble did not differ significantly between SNR conditions.
source: whereas P2-N1 amplitudes for babble did not differ significantly between SNR conditions (all pHolm > 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through post-hoc analysis of TRF data in Experiment 3.

claim: The results of Experiment 3 show that neural speech tracking increases for babble and speech-matched noise maskers compared to clear speech.
source: The results of Experiment 3 show that neural speech tracking increases for babble and speech-matched noise maskers compared to clear speech
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 3.

claim: The results of Experiment 3 show that the 12-talker babble masker leads to a greater enhancement compared to the speech-matched noise.
source: but that the 12-talker babble masker leads to a greater enhancement compared to the speech-matched noise.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 3.

claim: Slight variations in the level of the speech signal in the sound mixture (resulting from different sound-level normalization procedures) do not seem to overly impact the results.
source: Slight variations in the level of the speech signal in the sound mixture (resulting from different sound-level normalization procedures) do not seem to overly impact the results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 4, participants listened to stories in quiet (clear) or in the presence of different types of background maskers at +20 dB SNR.
source: In Experiment 4, participants listened to stories in quiet (clear) or in the presence of different types of background maskers at +20 dB SNR while EEG was recorded.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, masker types included stationary noise that spectrally matched the speech signal, white noise, pink noise, 12-talker babble, and three newly created 12-talker babbles.
source: Masker types included stationary noise that spectrally matched the speech signal (Experiment 3), white noise, pink noise, 12-talker babble (Experiments 1–3), and three newly created 12-talker babbles.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, comprehension accuracy and gist ratings for the clear story did not significantly differ from the data for masked speech.
source: Comprehension accuracy and gist ratings for the clear story did not significantly differ from the data for masked speech (for all pFDR > 0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, EEG prediction accuracy did not significantly differ between clear speech and any of the masker types.
source: EEG prediction accuracy did not significantly differ between clear speech and any of the masker types (for all pFDR > 0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of EEG data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the TRF P1-N1 amplitude was larger for all masker types, except for white noise, compared to clear speech.
source: In contrast, the TRF P1-N1 amplitude was larger for all masker types, expect for white noise, compared to clear speech (for all pFDR ≤ 0.05; Figure 6D; the difference between clear speech and speech masked by white noise was significant when uncorrected; p = 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, there were no differences among the four different babble maskers.
source: There were no differences among the four different babble maskers (for all p > 0.6), indicating that different voice genders of the 12-talker babble do not differentially affect the masker-related enhancement in neural speech tracking.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the P1-N1 amplitude was larger for speech masked by the babble maskers (collapsed across the four babble maskers) compared to speech masked by white noise.
source: However, the P1-N1 amplitude was larger for speech masked by the babble maskers (collapsed across the four babble maskers) compared to speech masked by white noise (t19 = 4.133, p = 5.7 ∙ 10–4, d = 0.68)
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the P1-N1 amplitude was larger for speech masked by the babble maskers compared to speech masked by pink noise.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the P1-N1 amplitude was larger for speech masked by the babble maskers compared to speech masked by the noise that spectrally matched to speech.
source: and the noise that spectrally matched to speech (t19 = 3.039, p = 0.007, d = 0.68).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, there were no differences among the three noise maskers.
source: There were no differences among the three noise maskers (for all p > 0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the P2-N1 amplitude for clear speech did not differ from the P2-N1 amplitude for masked speech.
source: The P2-N1 amplitude for clear speech did not differ from the P2-N1 amplitude for masked speech (for all pFDR > 0.05; Figure 6D, right).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of TRF data in Experiment 4.

claim: The results of Experiment 4 replicate the results from Experiments 1–3 by showing that babble noise at a high SNR (20 dB) increases neural speech tracking.
source: The results of Experiment 4 replicate the results from Experiments 1–3 by showing that babble noise at a high SNR (20 dB) increases neural speech tracking.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 4.

claim: Experiment 4 shows that the neural-tracking enhancement generalizes across different noises, albeit a bit less for white noise.
source: Experiment 4 further shows that the neural-tracking enhancement generalizes across different noises, albeit a bit less for white noise (significant only when uncorrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 4.

claim: Stochastic resonance has been described as the facilitation of a near-threshold input through noise.
source: Stochastic resonance has been described as the facilitation of a near-threshold input through noise. That is, a near-threshold stimulus or neuronal input, that alone may be insufficient to drive a neuron beyond its firing threshold, can lead to neuronal firing if noise is added, because the noise increases the stimulus or neuronal input for brief periods, causing a response in downstream neurons (Ward et al., 2002; Moss et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The term stochastic resonance is now used more broadly to describe any phenomenon where the presence of noise in a non-linear system improves the quality of the output signal than when noise is absent.
source: However, the term is now used more broadly to describe any phenomenon where the presence of noise in a non-linear system improves the quality of the output signal than when noise is absent (McDonnell and Abbott, 2009).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to previous research.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.
